tldr: This paper extracts contact appearance, geometry (normal/depth), and tangential deformation (marker flow) from a single vision-based tactile sensor stream and thoroughly clarifies which physical cues truly matter for imitation learning through 720 real-robot trials.
hero_caption: An overview of the entire study concept. Three physical cues—tactile RGB appearance, normal/depth maps, and marker displacement fields—are extracted from the same tactile sensor stream. Cue types, encoders, and fusion methods are rigorously compared on a shared pipeline combining LeRobot and Diffusion Policy.
overview:
In contact-rich tasks where a robot securely grasps, assembles, or wipes objects, tactile sensing is indispensable for understanding what happens in camera occlusions. In recent years, vision-based tactile sensors (such as GelSight) that capture elastomer deformation using an internal camera have been widely adopted. However, most imitation learning methods simply feed the acquired tactile images directly into a CNN as standard RGB images. As a result, it has remained a black box which physical information—contact surface appearance, geometry like indentation depth and surface normals, or tangential displacement and friction (tangential deformation)—actually contributes to policy success.

To address this, the authors built a system that disentangles and extracts appearance (RGB), geometry (normal/depth), and tangential deformation (marker flow) from the exact same tactile stream. A major strength of their setup is a controlled benchmark built upon LeRobot, an open-source robot learning framework, combined with Diffusion Policy, keeping demonstration data, network capacity, and training conditions completely identical.

Across 720 real-robot evaluation trials, introducing tactile sensing substantially boosted the overall success rate from 57.8% to 78.9%. Among individual cues, marker flow derived from marker motion proved the most effective, reaching 74.4%. Furthermore, the study uncovered distinct stage-dependent roles: contact geometry is critical during the initial contact establishment phase, whereas marker flow shines in regulating and maintaining established contact forces.
contributions: Built an open real-robot evaluation platform compatible with LeRobot that disentangles appearance (RGB), contact geometry (normal/depth), and tangential deformation (marker flow) from an identical tactile data stream.

Demonstrated through 720 real-robot trials that marker flow is the most effective individual cue, and showed that different physical cues are required across distinct contact phases (establishing contact vs. maintaining contact).

Showed that cue-factorized encoding—processing each physical cue through dedicated frontends rather than treating the tactile observation as a monolithic RGB image—is crucial for boosting performance.
Revealed that in visuo-tactile fusion, cross-attention offers a lightweight mechanism capable of achieving performance comparable to large pretrained tactile encoders (such as Sparsh).

sections.heading: Why shouldn't we treat tactile images as "just another camera image"?
sections.summary: While tactile sensing is a powerful modality in contact-rich manipulation, most existing studies treat tactile images just like standard camera frames. This section discusses why disentangling the diverse physical cues embedded in tactile observations—appearance, geometry, and deformation—is essential to determine what truly benefits policy learning.
sections.details:
Visuomotor policies that learn robot behaviors from camera inputs have advanced remarkably. However, they face inherent limitations when hands occlude objects or when tiny contact events and slippages must be detected. Consequently, vision-based tactile sensors that directly observe local contact states have drawn significant attention.

Yet, an important oversight has persisted. Images captured by a tactile sensor conflate fundamentally different physical phenomena: surface texture and illumination changes (appearance), indentation depth and surface relief (contact geometry), and shear strain from surface rubber being dragged sideways (tangential deformation). Most existing methods feed these signals into CNNs as single images without distinction, leaving it unclear which physical features actually drive policy success.

To tackle this, the authors designed a controlled study extracting three distinct physical representations from the same sensor data, using identical demonstrations, observations, and policy backbones (Diffusion Policy) for a fair comparison. Knowing which cues matter provides critical design guidelines not just for policy architectures, but also for future tactile sensor hardware development.

sections.heading: A brief look at tactile hardware, imitation learning, and representation learning
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of vision-based tactile sensors like GelSight and DIGIT, alongside recent trends in tactile imitation learning. It positions the current study against prior work in self-supervised tactile representations (such as Sparsh) and multimodal fusion, emphasizing its unique role in providing a controlled comparison of physical cues from identical inputs.
sections.details:
### Lineages of Vision-Based Tactile Sensors
Vision-based tactile sensors primarily follow two designs: photometric sensors (such as GelSight) that precisely reconstruct 3D surface geometry using computational photometric stereo, and marker-based sensors (such as FingerVision) that track dots embedded inside an elastomer to detect forces and slips. While hybrid sensors combining both approaches have recently emerged, it remained unverified which information is genuinely necessary for learning.

### Visuo-Tactile Learning for Contact-Rich Tasks
To integrate tactile data into manipulation policies, researchers have explored slow-fast loops for high-frequency tactile responses and learning from multimodal human demonstrations. However, these systems relied on fixed sensor representations without comparing individual physical cues under controlled settings.

### Tactile Representation Learning and Multimodal Fusion
Recent works have introduced self-supervised pretraining on massive tactile datasets (Sparsh), invariant representations across sensor variations (SITR), and cross-attention architectures linking vision and touch (ViTacFormer). This study complements these cutting-edge efforts by benchmarking pretrained models and attention-based fusion mechanisms under a unified framework of disentangled physical cues.

sections.heading: How to extract three physical cues from a single tactile video stream
sections.summary: This section describes the real-robot setup extending LeRobot and the pipeline used to derive tactile RGB, normal/depth maps, and marker flow from the same tactile stream. It also details the Diffusion Policy backbone, cue-factorized encoder architectures, and visuo-tactile fusion strategies.
sections.details:
### Hardware Configuration and Data Collection Platform
A parallel gripper was equipped on one finger with a GelSight Wedge-style tactile sensor featuring marker-embedded elastomer, an internal camera, and calibrated LED illumination (the opposing finger serves as a passive support surface). An external third-person camera, a wrist camera, robot joint proprioception, and tactile video streams are synchronously recorded at millisecond precision within the LeRobot framework.

### Derivation of Three Physical Tactile Cues
From a single tactile camera stream, the authors derive three distinct representations:
- **Tactile RGB**: The raw RGB frame $I_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ is used directly, containing contact surface texture and lighting variations.
- **Contact Geometry**: Surface normal maps $N_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ are estimated from difference images (relative to an uncontacted reference) using a neural calibration network. Poisson reconstruction then integrates these normals into an indentation depth map $D_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 1}$. The combined input is the channel-concatenated $[N_t, D_t]$.
- **Tangential Deformation**: Displacements $\Delta m_t^i$ of dots embedded in the elastomer relative to their initial positions are tracked and interpolated into a dense marker-flow field $F_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 2}$. This directly reflects tangential forces and shear displacements.

In addition to evaluating each cue individually, a "Full tactile" configuration $\{I_t, [N_t, D_t], F_t\}$ processes all three cues in parallel using dedicated, specialized frontends.

### Policy and Fusion Architectures
The policy backbone uses Diffusion Policy, which generates action sequences by iteratively denoising random trajectories. Conditioning on an observation history of the past 4 steps, the model predicts future 24-step action sequences, executing the first 8 steps before replanning. Under the full tactile setting, the authors compare a standard ResNet-18 against a tactile-pretrained "Sparsh-DINO" encoder for tactile RGB, alongside two fusion strategies with wrist-camera features: simple concatenation versus cross-attention.

captions.P3: The overall system and Diffusion Policy pipeline (Fig. 2). Each visual and tactile modality is processed by a dedicated encoder. When enabled, cross-attention connects the wrist camera and tactile RGB before features are integrated into a 1D U-Net for action generation.
captions.P4: Internal sensor construction (left: Fig. 3) and extracted tactile representations (right: Fig. 4). For the same contacted objects (scissors, screw, USB flash drive), RGB images, depth maps, surface normal maps, and marker-flow fields are cleanly disentangled.

sections.heading: 720 real-robot trials: what works, and why policies fail
sections.summary: A total of 720 trials were carried out across three real-robot manipulation tasks: tube reorientation and insertion, blackboard wiping, and peg-in-hole insertion. The authors analyze the overall impact of tactile sensing, individual cue effectiveness, stage-dependent failure modes, and combinations of encoders and fusion mechanisms.
sections.details:
### Experimental Tasks
Evaluation focused on three challenging tasks involving diverse contact dynamics:
1. **Tube Reorientation**: Sliding and pivoting a test tube inside the fingertips to adjust its orientation, followed by inserting it into a rack. This demands sensitivity to localized slip and in-hand regrasping.
2. **Blackboard Wiping**: Sliding an eraser across a blackboard while maintaining a steady normal contact force. Regulating normal pressure and tangential friction is crucial.
3. **Peg-in-hole Insertion**: Inserting a peg into a tight-clearance socket. Small alignment errors cause mechanical jamming.
Each task and condition was evaluated over 30 trials, totaling 720 real-robot runs.

### Comparative Results Across Cues
- **Overall Tactile Impact**: Tactile perception raised the overall success rate from 57.8% (52/90) with vision-only to 78.9% (71/90) with full tactile sensing—a substantial 21.1-percentage-point gain. In the tube task, the boost was especially pronounced, climbing 30 points from 46.7% to 76.7%.
- **The Strongest Individual Cue**: Marker flow led all single-cue baselines with a 74.4% success rate (67/90). Tactile RGB achieved 73.3%, while geometry (normal/depth) reached 66.7%.
- **The Value of Full Tactile Sensing**: While full tactile (78.9%) scored only slightly higher than marker flow alone (74.4%) in aggregate numbers, it produced noticeably smoother, more continuous transitions from initial contact to task completion. Factorizing physical cues into dedicated network branches clearly outperformed feeding raw RGB directly into a single model.

### Qualitative Failure Mode Analysis (Stage-Dependent Roles)
Scrutinizing failed runs revealed a revealing pattern:
- **Normal/Depth (Geometry)**: Highly effective at guiding initial contact formation, but prone to stalling or getting stuck during subsequent sliding, dragging, or pivoting phases where contact had to be maintained and regulated.
- **Marker Flow (Tangential Deformation)**: Outstanding at regulating forces and handling sustained sliding, but more vulnerable to initial grasp misalignments (which caused jamming in peg insertion).
In short, geometry governs contact *establishment*, while marker flow governs contact *regulation and maintenance*.

### Encoder and Fusion Strategy Comparisons
Under the full tactile setting, simply adding cross-attention to a standard ResNet-18 boosted the success rate from 78.9% to 85.6%. This outperformed using the pretrained Sparsh-DINO model with simple concatenation (83.3%). Combining Sparsh-DINO with cross-attention yielded the top performance of 87.8%. Nevertheless, for setups with limited computing resources, cross-attention provides a remarkably lightweight way to capture strong multimodal benefits.

captions.P5: Successful trajectories across the three tasks (left) and representative failure cases tied to specific tactile cues (right: Fig. 5). Policies relying on normal/depth often stalled after initial contact, whereas marker-flow policies occasionally misgrasped objects during early phases, showing clear temporal differences in failure modes.

sections.heading: Conclusions and practical takeaways for tactile robot learning
sections.summary: This section summarizes the key findings and practical design principles for tactile imitation learning. It also addresses the study's limitations—such as the absence of direct force sensing and reliance on a single sensor geometry—and highlights directions for future research.
sections.details:
This work represents the first systematic real-robot study to disentangle vision-based tactile signals and rigorously evaluate their physical contributions to imitation learning.

The practical takeaways are clear. First, practitioners should avoid feeding tactile images blindly as raw RGB; factorizing observations into distinct physical cues with dedicated frontends yields clear performance benefits. Second, when resource constraints permit only a single cue, marker flow capturing tangential deformation is the most capable choice. Finally, even without large tactile-pretrained encoders, introducing cross-attention between wrist vision and tactile features provides a lightweight, highly effective boost.

The authors also acknowledge several limitations:
- Ground-truth force and torque measurements from 6-axis F/T sensors were not recorded for direct quantitative validation.
- Encoders for image inputs (ResNet) and marker flow (MLP) differed in architecture, leaving open whether representation or network capacity drove minor gaps.
- Experiments were limited to a single sensor design (GelSight Wedge), a parallel-jaw gripper, and three tabletop tasks.
Future investigations are expected to extend this methodology to multi-fingered hands and assess cross-sensor generalizability.

takeaways: Move beyond treating tactile images as monolithic RGB frames; factorize them into physical cues like geometry and tangential deformation, processing each through a specialized frontend.
Marker flow is the most cost-effective single cue, showing unmatched stability in regulating forces and slip once contact is established.
Geometry (normal/depth) excels at establishing contact, while marker flow excels at maintaining and regulating contact. Combining both enables smooth execution across the full manipulation sequence.
Even without large pretrained tactile representations (like Sparsh), adding a lightweight cross-attention layer between wrist vision and tactile features delivers comparable or superior performance.
limitations: No direct quantitative force or torque ground-truth was measured using external F/T sensors.
Because visual inputs used CNNs while marker flows used MLPs, performance differences cannot be attributed purely to input representations alone.

The evaluation was restricted to a single sensor model (GelSight Wedge), a parallel two-finger gripper, and three tabletop tasks, leaving multi-fingered hands and diverse sensor geometries for future work.
